clinicalScope: Placenta praevia in pregnant women in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Placenta Praevia
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Placenta praevia is a low‑lying or covering placenta that causes painless ante‑partum bleeding. Diagnosis relies on history, bedside exam and limited ultrasound. Management centres on avoiding digital exam, planning delivery and controlling bleeding.

sections.p: Placenta praevia is the placenta lying over or within 2 cm of the internal cervical os. It presents with painless, bright‑red bleeding after 20 weeks. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound when available.
b: Painless, bright‑red bleeding
No pain on palpation
Bleeding after 20 weeks

t.b: Placenta over os = praevia; within 2 cm = low‑lying

sections.p: Placenta praevia is staged by distance from the os:
b: Grade I – placenta over os, <2 cm from os
Grade II – placenta 2–3 cm from os
Grade III – placenta 3–5 cm from os
Grade IV – placenta >5 cm from os (low‑lying)

sections.p: Risk factors are cumulative and often overlap in low‑resource settings.
b: Previous caesarean section or uterine surgery
Multiparity (≥3 births)
Advanced maternal age (>35 y)
History of placenta praevia
Previous uterine curettage
Use of herbal uterotonics
Infections causing uterine scarring (e.g., TB, schistosomiasis) – less common but present

sections.p: The classic presentation is painless, bright‑red bleeding that may stop and start. Patients are usually well‑tolerated until bleeding is massive.
b: Painless, bright‑red bleeding
No abdominal pain or cramping
Bleeding may be intermittent

sections.p: Investigations are limited by resource availability. Prioritise those that change management.
b: CBC – haemoglobin to gauge blood loss
Transabdominal ultrasound – placental location
Blood group & crossmatch – prepare for transfusion

t.b: If unavailable, rely on history and exam

sections.p: Urgent red flags require immediate transfer to a higher‑level facility.
b: Continuous heavy bleeding
Fetal distress on monitoring
Maternal haemodynamic instability
Signs of placenta accreta (e.g., previous scar, abnormal ultrasound)

sections.p: Management is staged by severity and resource setting.
b: Avoid digital vaginal examination until praevia excluded
If bleeding stops, hospitalise and monitor
For Grade I–II: plan elective caesarean at 36–37 weeks
For Grade III–IV or uncontrolled bleeding: emergency caesarean
Use oxytocin infusion post‑delivery to prevent PPH
Avoid prostaglandins before delivery – they may induce contractions and worsen bleeding

t.b: Start 10 U in 1 L saline, 1 mL/min, titrate to tone

sections.p: Post‑delivery care focuses on haemostasis and counselling for future pregnancies.
b: Transfuse if anaemic
Monitor for infection
Counsel on avoiding uterotonics before labour
Plan repeat caesarean in future pregnancies if placenta praevia recurs

faq.q: Why is digital vaginal examination contraindicated in suspected placenta praevia?
faq.a: It can trigger massive bleeding by disturbing the placenta over the os.

faq.q: What is the safest uterotonic after caesarean for placenta praevia?
faq.a: Oxytocin infusion – it promotes uterine contraction without stimulating the uterus before delivery.

faq.q: Can a low‑lying placenta be managed expectantly?
faq.a: Only if it is >5 cm from the os and the patient is haemodynamically stable; otherwise delivery is planned.

exam: What is the first step in a woman with painless bleeding after 24 weeks? — Obtain history, avoid digital exam, arrange ultrasound; early identification prevents catastrophic bleeding.

How would you differentiate placenta praevia from retained products of conception? — Placenta praevia shows placenta over os on ultrasound; retained products respond to curettage and show no placenta on scan.

Why is oxytocin preferred over prostaglandins for uterine contraction after delivery in placenta praevia? — Oxytocin contracts the uterus without stimulating it before delivery, reducing risk of bleeding.
What is the management of a patient with Grade II placenta praevia who is haemodynamically unstable? — Emergency caesarean with blood products ready; avoid digital exam.
What is the role of tranexamic acid in placenta praevia? — Given within 3 h of delivery it reduces blood loss and need for transfusion.
How do you counsel a woman who had placenta praevia about future pregnancies? — Advise planned caesarean at 36–37 weeks and discuss risks of accreta and uterine rupture.
